title: ⟨Αἰσχρὰ⟩ δούλη καὶ Ἀφροδίτη
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 18. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Αἰσχρᾶς καὶ κακοτρόπου δούλης ἤρα δεσπότης.
sentences.tr: Aischras kai kakotropou doulēs ēra despotēs.
sentences.l: A master was in love with an ugly and ill-natured slave-woman.
sentences.n: ἐράω takes the genitive of the person loved. αἰσχρός means “ugly” of the body and “shameful” of conduct, and the fable works both senses at once — the epimythium comes back to it with δι' αἰσχρά. In the title Chambry prints ⟨Αἰσχρά⟩ inside angle brackets: those mark words he supplies that the manuscripts do not have. Square brackets, which appear in this fable's moral, mark the opposite — words he judges a later addition and deletes.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ χρυσίον λαμβάνουσα λαμπρῶς ἑαυτὴν ἐκόσμει καὶ τῇ ἰδίᾳ δεσποίνῃ μάχας συνῆπτε· τῇ δὲ Ἀφροδίτῃ ἔθυεν συνεχῶς καὶ ηὔχετο ὡς ὡραίαν αὐτὴν ποιούσῃ.
sentences.tr: Hē de chrysion lambanousa lamprōs heautēn ekosmei kai tēi idiāi despoinēi machas synēpte· tēi de Aphroditēi ethyen synechōs kai ēucheto hōs hōraian autēn poiousēi.
sentences.l: And she, receiving gold, adorned herself splendidly and joined battles with her own mistress; and she sacrificed to Aphrodite continually and prayed to her as to one making her beautiful.
sentences.i: With the gold she was given she decked herself out splendidly and picked quarrels with her own mistress; and she sacrificed to Aphrodite without let-up and prayed to her as the one who was making her lovely.
sentences.n: μάχας συνάπτω, “join battles”, is the plain idiom for picking a fight. ὡς with a participle gives the reason as the person concerned sees it, not as a fact: ποιούσῃ is dative, agreeing with Aphrodite, so the sense is “on the ground that she was the one making her beautiful.” Aphrodite is the goddess of beauty and desire, and a woman would naturally vow and sacrifice to her for looks — which is what makes the goddess's answer a rebuke rather than a refusal.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ καθ’ ὕπνου φανεῖσα τῇ δούλῃ ἔφη μὴ ἔχειν αὐτῇ χάριν ὡς καλὴν αὐτὴν ποιούσῃ, « ἀλλ’ ἐκείνῳ θυμοῦμαι καὶ ὀργίζομαι ᾧ σὺ φαίνῃ καλή. »
sentences.tr: Hē de kath’ hypnou phaneisa tēi doulēi ephē mē echein autēi charin hōs kalēn autēn poiousēi, « all’ ekeinōi thymoumai kai orgizomai hōi sy phainēi kalē. »
sentences.l: And she, having appeared in sleep to the slave-woman, said that the woman owed her no gratitude as to one making her beautiful, « but I am angry and enraged at that man to whom you appear beautiful. »
sentences.i: But Aphrodite appeared to her in her sleep and told her she had no thanks owing to the goddess, as though it were Aphrodite who was making her beautiful: « No — it is that man I am angry and furious with, the one in whose eyes you seem beautiful. »
sentences.n: The sentence begins in indirect speech (ἔφη… ἔχειν) and slides into the goddess's own words; Chambry marks the change with guillemets. That slide is common in Greek and needs no signal in the original. χάριν ἔχειν τινί is fixed, “to owe gratitude to someone”. The infinitive has no expressed subject, so the referents have to be read off the previous sentence, which is built the same way: αὐτῇ and ποιούσῃ are both Aphrodite, and the one who owes the thanks is the slave-woman. The goddess is refusing the credit for the woman's looks, not the offerings. καθ' ὕπνου, “in sleep”, is how a god answers a prayer in these stories, by appearing in a dream; the genitive after κατά is odd, the phrase being normally καθ' ὕπνον. φαίνῃ is second singular middle, “you appear, you seem”.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ τυφοῦσθαι τοὺς δι’ αἰσχρὰ πλουτοῦντας καὶ μάλιστα, εἰ ἀγενεῖς εἰσι καὶ ἄμορφοι [πρὸς αἰσχύνην μείζονα].
sentences.tr: Hoti ou dei typhousthai tous di’ aischra ploutountas kai malista, ei ageneis eisi kai amorphoi [pros aischynēn meizona].
sentences.l: That those who grow rich by shameful means ought not to be puffed up, and especially if they are low-born and misshapen [to their greater shame].
sentences.i: Those who grow rich by shameful means should not give themselves airs — least of all if they are low-born and ill-favoured [which only makes the disgrace the greater].
sentences.n: Chambry brackets [πρὸς αἰσχύνην μείζονα] as an interpolation: words a later hand added, which he prints but deletes. The text is a reconstruction and the brackets are where the seams show. τυφοῦσθαι is literally “to be smoked up”, the regular Greek for swelling with conceit. Like fable 16, the moral opens with a bare Ὅτι leaning on an unspoken “the story shows…”.
